stem:
Read the extract and study the data. Dube Furniture (Pvt) Ltd is a fictional business.

**Dube Furniture (Pvt) Ltd, Mutare.** Mr Dube started the business ten years ago as a sole trader, making beds and wardrobes from timber. Four years ago he formed a private limited company, owned by himself and two relatives, so that his house would not be at risk when he borrowed to buy machines. The company makes furniture in a small factory and sells it to shops and directly to households in the region. Sales and the number of workers have risen each year, but timber prices have increased and a large importer has cut prices, so Dube Furniture has had to keep its own prices low. The directors now have two choices for a new cutting machine costing US\$60,000: borrow the money from a bank, or sell a 30% share of the company to an outside investor.

|  | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Sales (US\$) | 310,000 | 342,000 | 372,000 |
| Profit for the year (US\$) | 32,550 | 30,780 | 29,760 |
| Number of employees | 31 | 34 | 38 |
| Total sales in the regional furniture market (US\$) | 1,480,000 | 1,520,000 | 1,550,000 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Size and sector

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: In which sector does Dube Furniture mainly operate?

options.rationale: Correct: it manufactures furniture from timber.
Primary firms grow or extract natural resources.
Quaternary firms deal in knowledge and information.

parts.label: (ii)

parts.stem: Calculate sales per employee in Year 3, to the nearest dollar.

parts.stem: Which statement best describes the trend in Dube Furniture's results?

options.content: Sales and profit have both risen every year
Sales have risen but profit has fallen
options.rationale: Correct: sales rose from US\$310,000 to US\$372,000 while profit fell from US\$32,550 to US\$29,760.

options.content: Sales and profit have both fallen every year
Sales have fallen but profit has risen

parts.explanation: Sales are up 20.0% but profit is down, so the profit margin has fallen from 10.5% to 8.0%.

parts.stem: Ownership

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Complete the sentence about the shareholders of Dube Furniture (Pvt) Ltd.

payload.template: The shareholders of a private limited company have {{blank:a}} liability, so they can lose no more than the money they have {{blank:b}}.

parts.explanation: Limited liability protects personal property; the loss is limited to the amount invested.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Explain why Mr Dube formed a company instead of continuing as a sole trader.

points.description: As a sole trader he had unlimited liability, so his house would be at risk when he borrowed
As a company, the shareholders' liability is limited to their investment, which protects his house

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: As a sole trader Mr Dube had unlimited liability and could lose his house if the business failed. As a private limited company, his liability is limited to his investment, so he can borrow without risking his home.

parts.explanation: Liability before and after.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Analyse **two** reasons why Dube Furniture's profit has fallen although its sales have risen.

points.description: Timber prices have increased, so costs have risen
Development: if costs rise faster than sales, profit falls (profit as a percentage of sales has fallen from 10.5% to 8.0%)
A large importer has cut prices, so Dube has had to keep its prices low
Development: lower prices reduce the profit earned on each piece of furniture even when more is sold

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Timber prices have risen, so costs have increased; if costs rise faster than sales, profit falls, which is why profit as a percentage of sales has fallen from 10.5% to 8.0%. A large importer has also cut prices, so Dube has had to keep its prices low, which reduces the profit on each piece of furniture even though more is sold.

parts.explanation: Two reasons, each developed using the data.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Advise the directors whether to finance the new machine by a bank loan or by selling 30% of the company to an outside investor. Justify your answer.

points.description: Bank loan: the owners keep full control and all the profit
Bank loan: interest and repayments must be paid even though profit is falling
Investor: no repayments and risk is shared
Investor: the family owners lose 30% of the control and profit
Judgement with a reason supported by the data, e.g. falling profit margin makes fixed repayments risky, so the investor may be safer if the family accepts losing some control

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A bank loan would let the family keep full control and all the profit, but interest and repayments would have to be paid even though the profit margin has fallen from 10.5% to 8.0%, which is risky. An investor would remove the need for repayments and share the risk, but the family would lose 30% of the control and of future profit. Because profit is falling, I would advise selling the 30% share, provided the family can accept an outsider's say in decisions; if control matters most, a smaller loan could be used instead.

parts.explanation: A reasoned recommendation using the data.

explanation: Secondary sector; sales growth 20.0%; market share 24.0%; US\$9,789 per employee; margin down from 10.5% to 8.0%; limited liability; costs and price competition; investor or loan weighed.

stem:
Read the case study (a fictional business) and answer all the questions.

**Ncube Mushrooms, Gweru.** Thandeka Ncube grows oyster mushrooms in two small sheds behind her house and sells them fresh to restaurants and supermarkets. She is a sole trader and employs three part-time workers. Last year her sales were US\$99,000 compared with US\$81,000 the year before, in a regional mushroom market worth US\$495,000 a year. A large farm in another province has begun to sell in the same market at lower prices.

Thandeka wants to build two more sheds. Her business plan gives the start-up costs below. She has US\$6,500 of her own money. The bank will lend the rest only if she offers her house as security. She expects to sell each kilogram for US\$4.80, the variable cost is US\$2.40 a kilogram and fixed costs are US\$960 a month. She forecasts sales of 650 kg a month. Her cousin Sipho has offered to join her as a partner, put in US\$7,500 and share profits equally.

| Start-up cost for the expansion | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Two new growing sheds | 6,400 |
| Shelving and trays | 2,300 |
| First batch of spawn and substrate | 2,600 |
| Licence | 180 |
| Working capital | 2,520 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Business activity and ownership

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: In which sector is the growing of mushrooms?

options.rationale: Correct: growing is a primary activity.

parts.explanation: Growing crops is primary production.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: What kind of liability does Thandeka have for the debts of her business?

options.rationale: Limited liability belongs to company shareholders.
The owner is liable for debts.
Customers are not liable for the owner's debts.
Correct: as a sole trader she is personally liable.

parts.explanation: A sole trader has unlimited liability.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: Complete the sentence about a sole trader.

payload.template: A sole trader keeps all the {{blank:a}} but has {{blank:b}} liability for debts.

parts.explanation: The owner receives all the profit but is personally liable without limit.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Business plan figures

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the total funding required for the expansion.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Calculate the amount Thandeka would need to borrow if she uses only her own money and a bank loan.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: Calculate the monthly break-even output in kilograms.
parts.explanation: Contribution = 4.80 − 2.40 = 2.40. Break-even = 960 ÷ 2.40 = 400 kg.

parts.label: (iv)
parts.stem: Calculate the margin of safety as a percentage of forecast sales (650 kg), to one decimal place.
parts.explanation: (650 − 400) ÷ 650 × 100 = 38.5%. Dividing by break-even output gives 62.5%.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Size and growth

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate Ncube Mushrooms' market share last year, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage growth in sales over last year, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain **two** problems that Ncube Mushrooms is likely to face as a small business.

points.description: Finance: the bank will lend only against her house, so she cannot expand without risking her home
Development: she cannot buy the extra sheds without the money, so growth is slowed
Competition: a large farm sells at lower prices
Development: large farms can buy inputs in bulk and have lower costs, so she may lose customers or have to cut her price

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Finance is a problem: the bank will lend only if she offers her house, so she cannot expand without risking her home, and her growth is slowed. A large farm is selling at lower prices; large farms buy inputs in bulk and have lower costs, so Thandeka may lose customers or have to cut her price.

parts.explanation: Two problems, each developed.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why the bank would want to see Thandeka's business plan before it lends to her.

points.description: The plan shows how the loan will be used and what the expansion will cost
Development: the bank can see that total funding is US\$14,000
The cash flow forecast and break-even show whether the loan could be repaid
Development: the break-even output is 400 kg against a forecast of 650 kg, a margin of safety of 38.5%, which lowers the bank's risk

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The plan shows how the loan will be used, since the expansion needs US\$14,000 in total. The break-even and forecast figures show whether the loan can be repaid: break-even is 400 kg a month against a forecast of 650 kg, a margin of safety of 38.5%, which lowers the bank's risk of not being repaid.

parts.explanation: Uses the figures in the plan.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Advise Thandeka whether she should borrow from the bank as a sole trader or take Sipho as a partner. Justify your answer.

points.description: Bank loan: she keeps control and all the profit
Bank loan: her house is at risk if the expansion fails (unlimited liability)
Partner: Sipho provides the US\$7,500 so no loan is needed
Partner: profits are shared equally and decisions must be shared
Partner: Sipho would also have unlimited liability and disagreements are possible, so a written agreement is needed
Judgement and reason, e.g. choose the partnership with a written agreement because it protects her house, if she is willing to share control

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A bank loan lets Thandeka keep control and all the profit, but she would have to put up her house, and as a sole trader she would be personally liable if the expansion failed. A partnership with Sipho avoids the loan because he provides US\$7,500, but profits and decisions would be shared equally and disagreements are possible; Sipho would also have unlimited liability. I would advise the partnership with a written agreement on duties, profit shares and what happens if a partner leaves, because it protects her house and the forecast margin of safety shows the expansion should be profitable; if she is unwilling to share control, she should borrow a smaller amount and expand more slowly.

parts.explanation: Both options judged with a conditional recommendation.

explanation: Funding US\$14,000; loan US\$7,500; break-even 400 kg; margin of safety 38.5%; market share 20.0%; sales growth 22.2%; problems of finance and competition; partnership or loan weighed.
hints: Add the start-up costs before finding the loan.
Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution per kilogram.

stem: Answer both parts of the question.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the main features of a private limited company.

points.description: It is a separate legal person from its owners
It can own property and make contracts in its own name
Ownership is divided into shares held by shareholders
Shareholders have limited liability: they can lose only what they invested
Their personal property cannot be claimed for the company's debts
Shares are sold privately and cannot be offered to the general public
Share transfer usually needs the agreement of the other owners
Directors, elected by the shareholders, run the company
The company continues if a shareholder dies or sells shares (continuity)
Profits are shared as dividends according to the number of shares held; the accounts are filed, with less disclosure than for a public company

levels.descriptor: Limited, mostly generic description with little accurate detail
Several accurate features described, some with development or an example
Wide, accurate and well-developed description of the topic with relevant examples

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
A private limited company is a separate legal person from its owners. It can own property and make contracts in its own name, and it can sue or be sued. Ownership is divided into shares, and the owners are shareholders. Their liability is limited: if the company fails, they lose only the money they invested, and their personal property cannot be claimed for the company's debts. This makes people more willing to invest.

The shares of a private company are sold privately and cannot be offered to the general public, and a shareholder who wants to sell usually needs the agreement of the other owners. The shareholders elect directors to run the company on their behalf, so in a small company the owners and directors are often the same people. The company has continuity: it carries on if a shareholder dies or sells shares. Profits are paid to shareholders as dividends in proportion to the shares they hold. A private company must file its accounts, but it has to disclose less than a public company.

parts.explanation: One mark for each accurate feature, developed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Discuss whether a successful sole trader should convert the business into a private limited company.

points.description: Limited liability protects the owner's personal property if the business fails
This encourages the owner to take risks and to borrow for growth
A company can raise capital by selling shares to investors
Capital from shares needs no repayments and may allow expansion without a bank loan
A company has continuity and a separate identity, so it can continue if the owner dies or retires
Lenders and customers may see a company as more established
Against: registration and legal costs are greater
Against: accounts must be filed, so there is less privacy
Against: more rules to follow on meetings, records and directors' duties
Against: if outside shareholders are admitted, the owner loses some control and shares profit
Against: lenders may still ask for personal guarantees, reducing the benefit of limited liability
Application: the benefit is greater when the business is growing, borrowing or holds large stock
Application: the move is less worthwhile for a small, low-risk business that needs no new capital
Judgement stated clearly
Justification: the decision depends on the size of the risk, the capital needed and the owner's willingness to share control

levels.descriptor: Mostly description or assertion; one side only; no judgement
Both sides developed, some application to the situation; judgement stated but weakly supported
Balanced, well-developed arguments applied to the situation and a justified judgement that depends on stated conditions

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
A sole trader has unlimited liability, so if the business fails the owner's house and savings can be used to pay its debts. Converting to a private limited company gives limited liability: the owner could lose only what was invested in shares. This protection encourages the owner to take risks and to borrow for growth. A company can also raise capital by selling shares to investors, which does not have to be repaid like a loan and may allow expansion without a bank loan. A company has continuity, because it carries on if the owner dies or retires, and lenders and customers may see it as more established.

However, there are costs. Registration and legal costs are greater, accounts must be filed so there is less privacy, and there are more rules on records and directors' duties. If outside shareholders are admitted, the owner loses some control and must share profit. Lenders may also ask for personal guarantees, which reduces the benefit of limited liability.

The benefit is greatest when the business is growing, borrowing heavily or carrying a lot of stock, so that the risk of large debts is real. For a small, low-risk business that needs no new capital, the extra cost and formality may not be worth it. On balance, a successful sole trader who wants to expand and borrow should convert, provided the owner can accept sharing some control and the extra costs; a stable business with little debt may stay as it is.

parts.explanation: Level descriptors apply: both sides, application and a justified judgement.

explanation: (a) features of a private limited company; (b) discussion of limited liability and capital against cost and loss of control.
hints: Describe features in (a); in (b) give both sides and a judgement.

stem: Answer both parts of the question.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the characteristics of a successful enterpriser.

points.description: Shows initiative: spots opportunities and acts on them
Willing to take calculated risks
Creative and innovative: finds new or better ways to meet needs
Determined and resilient: continues after failures
Self-confident: believes in the idea and persuades others
Organised and a good planner
Honest and ethical in dealing with customers and suppliers
Good with money: controls costs and records
A leader who can motivate workers
Willing to learn: from mistakes, training and customers

levels.descriptor: Limited, mostly generic description with little accurate detail
Several accurate features described, some with development or an example
Wide, accurate and well-developed description of the topic with relevant examples

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
A successful enterpriser shows initiative: she spots an opportunity, such as a need that local people cannot meet, and acts on it. She is willing to take calculated risks, investing time and money in an uncertain venture, but she plans carefully to keep the risk manageable. She is creative and innovative, looking for new or better ways to meet needs, and she is determined and resilient, carrying on after setbacks such as a failed crop or a lost customer.

She is self-confident, so she can persuade lenders, suppliers and customers. She is organised and a good planner, and she is good with money, controlling costs and keeping records. She is honest and ethical with customers and suppliers, which builds trust and repeat business. She leads and motivates the people who work for her, and she is willing to learn from mistakes, training and customers.

parts.explanation: One mark for each accurate characteristic, developed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Discuss whether the constraints on enterprises make enterprising not worthwhile.

points.description: Political constraints: changing policies on land, taxes and trade reduce confidence
Legal constraints: licences, registration and health rules add cost and delay
Economic constraints: high costs of power and transport, inflation and weak demand reduce profit
Social constraints: community attitudes, customs and crime can limit what a venture can do
Ecological constraints: limits on water and land use and the need to avoid pollution
These constraints can make some ventures unprofitable or force owners to give up
For: they affect smaller enterprisers more, who have fewer resources to cope
Against: enterprise still creates income and jobs even under constraints
Against: some constraints protect customers, workers and the environment, and improve the quality of the venture
Against: enterprisers can adapt by starting small, choosing a different venture or joining groups
Application: for example a vendor who must meet health rules can sell on safety and quality
Application: the benefits are greater where demand is strong and inputs are available locally
Judgement stated clearly
Justification: depends on the size of the constraint and the strength of the opportunity
Conclusion that links the judgement to the enterpriser's own qualities

levels.descriptor: Mostly description or assertion; one side only; no judgement
Both sides developed, some application to the situation; judgement stated but weakly supported
Balanced, well-developed arguments applied to the situation and a justified judgement that depends on stated conditions

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Enterprises face several constraints. Politically, changing policies on land, taxes and trade reduce confidence. Legally, licences, registration and health rules add cost and delay. Economically, high power and transport costs, inflation and weak demand reduce profit. Socially, community attitudes and crime can limit what a venture can do, and ecologically, limits on water and land use and the need to avoid pollution can restrict the size of an enterprise. Together these can make some ventures unprofitable and force owners to give up, and they affect small enterprisers most because they have few resources to absorb extra costs.

However, enterprising can still be worthwhile. Enterprise creates income and jobs even under constraints, and some constraints protect customers, workers and the environment and improve the quality of the venture. For example, a food vendor who must meet health rules can sell on safety and quality. Enterprisers can also adapt by starting small, choosing a different venture or joining groups to share costs.

On balance, constraints do not make enterprising pointless, but they make it more demanding. Enterprising is worthwhile where demand is strong, inputs are available locally and the enterpriser has the qualities to adapt; where a constraint is severe and the opportunity is weak, a different venture would be wiser.

parts.explanation: Level descriptors apply: both sides, application and a justified judgement.

explanation: (a) characteristics of an enterpriser; (b) discussion of constraints against the value of enterprising.
hints: Cover each type of constraint, then weigh them against the benefits of enterprising.
